messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
parts:
Hi,

I am running a model where n_eff is, for 99% of the parameters, equal to
the size of the posterior sample. This sounds too good to believe,
should I suspect something strange here? I devoted some thought to
coding the model in Stan (including some transformations), but this is
the first time I get so perfect sampling for a nontrivial model, so I
thought I would ask (I know that Stan is great, not questioning that
:D).

I ran the model on simulated data and everything is correctly estimated.

The exceptions are lp__ and three other variables, where n_eff is about
30-50% of the sample size, which is still great. Rhat is very good too.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
parts:
If you're using multiple diffuse random initializations and consistently getting good n_eff/Rhat and reliable estimation on simulated data then you're probably fine (and fortunate to have a nice model!).  The only major concern for me would be missed multimodality but if you're using multiple diffuse initializations then that should get caught by Rhat.  A potential secondary concern would be if the adaptation was too conservative and consequently you were only exploring a small part of the space and not capture variance and tail behaviour well, but again that would get picked up with multiple diffuse initializations.

So, in summary, confirm that you're using multiple diffuse starts (with different random seeds!) and then remember that Stan is awesome :)

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
parts:
A perfect n_eff is an overestimate, but hopefully not a bad overestimate. So, you are probably fine, although we can construct examples where it is not totally fine despite no divergent transitions. One such example is drawing from a multivariate t distribution with sufficiently large K (like 30) and sufficiently small degrees of freedom (like 5). The reason is that there is essentially no autocorrelation marginally but a lot of cross-parameter dependence due to the heavy tails.

Ben

P.S. Model:

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
  real<lower=0> nu;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[K,K] I;
  vector[K] zero;
  zero <- rep_vector(0.0, K);
  I <- rep_matrix(0.0, K, K);
  for(k in 1:K) I[k,k] <- 1.0;
}
parameters {
  vector[K] theta;
}
model {
  theta ~ multi_student_t(nu, zero, I);
}
generated quantities {
  real SS;
  SS <- dot_self(theta);
}

parts: If you have a t with low df, the whole “effective sample size” notion has problems, as we’ve defined it, because it’s based on means and variances. If you really want to get weird answers, try a Cauchy!

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: is a "perfect" n_eff suspicious?
parts:
On Thursday, November 20, 2014 4:09:30 PM UTC-5, Richard McElreath wrote:
Ben's example is fantastic for teaching.

I recall an example in maybe one of the Team's papers in which Rhat goes to 1 even though the chains are not converging. Or am I imagining that?

That happens in this example (among others), in the sense that different chains spend different amounts of time in the tails with the default number of iterations. I would say the chains have not converged, although they do happen to have the same mean and variance as the distribution they are converging to. So, your inferences might not be horrible if they don't depend too heavily on tail behavior. The following reparameterization of the "same" model but with independent primitives converges much better, but there is nothing in the Rhat or the n_eff or the n_divergent__ that would allow you to discern between the two.

data {
  int<lower=1> K;
  real<lower=0> nu;
}

parameters {                                                              
  vector[K] z;
  real<lower=0> u;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[K] theta;
  theta <- z ./ sqrt(u / nu);
}                                                                                            
model {
  z ~ normal(0,1);
  u ~ chi_square(nu);
  # implies theta ~ multi_normal_t(zero, I);

}
generated quantities {
  real SS;
  SS <- dot_self(theta);
}
